Peace to you as well, and thank you for the sincerity behind this question — you honor ʿĪsā and ask what honesty demands: did he himself claim this?

I'd push back gently on the idea that he only pointed away from himself. When he stood before his accusers and said, "Before Abraham was, I AM" — deliberately using the present tense ἐγὼ εἰμί that echoes God's own name at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14) — his hearers didn't hear a humble teacher. They took up stones, because they understood exactly what he was claiming: the Divine Name itself. That is about as plain as a first-century Jewish audience could receive such a claim, and it's why they responded with the charge of blasphemy, not confusion.

As for the disciples: when Thomas, touching the wounds of the risen Christ, said "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28) — not an exclamation of surprise but a direct confession of worship — Jesus did not correct him, deflect the praise, or say "worship God only, not me." He accepted it, and pronounced a blessing on all who would believe on the same testimony without Thomas's privilege of sight. If this were idolatry, the moment demanded correction; instead it received a benediction.

On the "why not more plainly" question — I take the difficulty seriously, and won't pretend it's trivial. But consider: a man walking among monotheistic Jews who announced outright "I am God, worship me" invites either instant execution as a blasphemer or a cult of shallow assent rather than tested faith. Instead he unveiled it gradually — through works only God does, claims only God could rightly make, and finally through the resurrection — so that the confession would be wrung out of genuine recognition, as it was from Thomas, rather than merely repeated as a slogan.

And his prayers, tears, hunger, and cry of forsakenness on the cross aren't evidence against divinity — they're exactly what you'd expect if the eternal Son had genuinely taken on real humanity, suffering as a man while remaining, in his own person, the one who could rightly receive Thomas's worship and bear the Name before which, per Philippians 2:5-11 echoing Isaiah 45, every knee bows. That two-natures shape — true God, true man — is precisely why he could both weep and be worshipped without contradiction.

transcript.content: Peace be upon you. You know, this troubles me greatly about Christian faith. We honor ʿĪsā deeply — the Messiah, born of the Virgin, given the Gospel, a spirit from God — but tell me: where did he ever say plainly, "I am God; worship me as God"? He prayed to God, he fasted, he wept, he asked "Why have you forsaken me?" — the actions of a servant, not the Creator. When the rich young man called him "good teacher," he turned it back: "Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone." If Jesus knew he was divine, why did he not say this clearly to his disciples, to the Jews, so that there could be no confusion about something so important? Instead, we find him pointing always *away* from himself, toward the One he served. The doctrine of his divinity — I say this with respect — seems to rest on interpretations and later councils, not on his own lips.
